title: Sacrifice The Knight!!! "OK, NP" | Three Knights Game | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We take White. Today is a defensive lesson — we're going to sacrifice a knight on purpose and show how to fight on when down material.
We develop the knight to c3, a Three Knights setup.
Black develops the bishop to c5. Our plan: sacrifice the knight — but not just yet.
We develop the bishop to c4.
Black plays d6.
Here's the sacrifice — the knight takes on e5, giving up the piece for at least a pawn.
Black recaptures, dxe5. Objectively we're a piece down and lost — but development isn't finished, so the plan is to complete it and make Black work for the win.
We play d3, part of finishing development — castle next, then start thinking in earnest.
Black plays the queen to f6, going for mate — and honestly that's encouraging: this walks into our hands.
We castle, defending f2. The trouble with the queen on f6 is that it invites a later knight to d5.

Black guards the square with the knight to e7. Now, the best defensive moves both improve your position and set a trap. The bishop to e3 is logical — if Black trades, we retake with the f-pawn and hit f7 from two sources. But there's something sharper: after the bishop to b3, Black plays ...Bb6 and comes to regret it.
We want f4 to prise open the f-file for chances — so first the king steps to h1, the classic preparation.
Black castles, and we're ready for f4.
We push f4, opening the file and stirring real intrigue on the kingside — the first progress in our counterplay.
Black captures on f4.
We must recapture with the bishop. Taking with the rook tempts you — it hits the queen — but attacking the queen isn't automatically good: the rook on f4 would be badly placed.
Black plays the queen to g6. Remember we're only a piece down — win three pawns for it and material is level.
So we take on c7 with the bishop, snapping off a pawn — pawns like that don't lie by the roadside.
Black pins with the bishop to g4. We must move the queen — to d2, or the interesting e1 to drag it toward the kingside.
The queen goes to d2. I avoid e1 because it runs into the knight rerouting to d4, and we want c2 guarded; from d2 the queen can also swing to f4 later.
Black jumps the knight to d4 — but it no longer carries a threat and hands us a free tempo.
We play the cryptic bishop to e5, pressing the knight on d4 — hoping Black obliges with the knight from e7 to c6.
Black finds the queen to h5 instead — a different, even stronger way of hitting our e5-bishop.
We drop the bishop back to g3 — where it was headed anyway, off the awkward c7-square and out of tactical trouble.
Black plays the knight to g6. My trick failed — yet it half-worked, because moving that knight has the same effect I was after.
Here's why I wanted that knight off e7: it guarded d5. Now we plant the knight on d5 and start building central pressure.
We were eyeing c3 next — but Black finds the knight to e2, a really nasty shot I missed. The bishop to f2 would defend, but ...Bd6 keeps the pressure; our emergency resource is the queen to e1.
So the queen to e1, forced — Black is playing superbly; that knight leap completely escaped me.
The knight takes on g3 with check — it was a mating threat — and we recapture with the queen. The trade actually helps us: Black has thinned his own attack, and now h3 is coming.
Black brings a rook to d8, setting a threat. We have two pawns for the piece — consolidate and we hold real chances.
The threat was ...Bd6, skewering the queen with mate to follow — so h3 must come at once, blunting it; if Black tries ...Bd6 anyway, we simply take the bishop on g4.
Black retreats the bishop to e6. Our sole trump is the central pawn mass Black doesn't have, so we must expand there.
We play c3, preparing to roll the centre with d4 and later e4–e5.
Black plays the bishop to d6. We're in deep trouble — ...Qe5 next is a serious problem.
We try the queen to f2 — a long shot, hoping to bait a sacrifice on h3.
Black takes the bait, sacrificing on h3.
We recapture, gxh3 — and I can't quite see where Black's mate is.
Black checks on h3, our king goes to g1 — and ...Nh4 is a bolt from the blue, threatening ...Nf3 with check and a mating net.

But there may be a defence. The knight lands on h4 threatening ...Nf3, which works only by pulling our queen off f2 — so we sidestep the queen. And here c3 pays off: a bishop to c5 now would allow d4, so if ...Nf3 comes we take it with the rook and keep control of h2. Black has a perpetual for a draw if he wants it — I'd gladly take that; what would truly worry me is a slow strengthening move like ...Re8.
